transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-11
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes (auto)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Olga Petrov (FjordBank Head Cloud Eng), Marcus Klein (CISO), Sana Iqbal (Compliance)

Auto-summary (automated, may be rough):
- FjordBank is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for EU data residency and HIPAA-ish financial PII controls.
- Primary concerns: where logs live, KMS/HSM key control, audit trails, data residency for R&D and backups, and vendor access during incident response.
- Next step: send compliance packet and schedule PoC kickoff with network diagram.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we got about 50 minutes. Quick round of intros please, just name and role so we can capture who says what.
[00:14] Olga Petrov: Olga, I run cloud eng at FjordBank. We manage a mix of GCP eu-west and some on-prem VMware for sensitive workloads.
[00:22] Marcus Klein: Marcus, CISO — primary focus is data residency, key separation, and minimizing vendor access vectors.
[00:30] Sana Iqbal: Sana, compliance manager, I'll be tracking SOC/HIPAA equivalency and retention rules.
[00:35] Maya Chen: Great, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood; Liam is our SE, he'll handle the technical deep-dive.
[00:40] Liam Ortiz: Hi all. Quick agenda: understand your compliance constraints, current stack, traffic profile, and then map Redwood's hosting options to your requirements — highlight logging and key management.

[01:05] Olga: Short version: We're building an internal assistant for front-line staff that touches KYC docs, partial account numbers, occasionally medical-like notes for eldercare products — legal says HIPAA-like safeguards, SOC2 and GDPR. We need to know if data stays in eu-west and where logs, KV cache, and backups are stored.
[01:30] Maya: Understood — common mix. A couple clarifying q's: are you allowed to send any PHI outside EU at all? And do you require customer-managed keys for everything or just for persistent storage?
[01:45] Marcus: No exports outside EU without DPA amendments. We also require customer-managed keys for stored embeddings and logs containing PII, but ephemeral inference cache in-memory is okay as long as it's zeroed and not persisted.
[02:05] Liam: That maps cleanly — Redwood Private gives you full control of the control plane and KMS; Dedicated can be configured in a VPC with KMS integration and restricted maintenance access. Hosted is the easiest but often requires contractual commitments for residency and a stricter review on key custody.
[02:30] Olga: Can you explain the difference in log handling between Dedicated and Private? Our audit team is picky about where syslogs and request logs land.
[02:40] Liam: Sure — Dedicated: the runtime runs in Redwood-managed infra reserved for you; we can export audit logs to your cloud logging endpoint in eu-west (you provide a logging sink), and we support routing application logs to your SIEM. Redwood engineers retain a reduced, redacted operational log set for debugging — those can be disabled or shipped to your S3/GCS bucket. Private: control plane is customer-managed, logs stay entirely in your network, and keys never leave your KMS/HSM.
[03:10] Marcus: Reduced, redacted operational logs — what exactly is kept? And for how long?
[03:18] Liam: Typically we keep metadata for incidents: request ids, timestamps, error codes — not prompt text — for 30 days by default on Dedicated, configurable down to 7 days. We can lengthen or export immediately to your retention store.
[03:35] Sana: Our policy is 7 years for certain financial audit trails. We cannot have prompt-level data stored for that timeframe in vendor-managed storage.
[03:45] Maya: That's common. For prompts containing PII you can opt into immediate streaming to your log sink or redact on the client before sending. Also, Redwood "prefix cache" is in-memory KV used for performance; that can be configured to avoid persisting sensitive prefixes.

[04:22] Olga: About backups and snapshots — if dedicated instances are in eu-west, are snapshots replicated outside region for resiliency?
[04:30] Liam: By default we replicate within the region. Cross-region backups are opt-in and would require a signed exception. For Private, backup behavior is under your control.
[04:45] Marcus: KMS: do you integrate with customer-managed KMS? We use an on-prem HSM for keys tied to legal obligations.
[04:52] Liam: Yes, Dedicated supports customer KMS integrations (Cloud KMS or on-prem via proxy). Private supports direct HSM attach where keys never traverse Redwood network. For hosted we can offer envelope encryption with keys we don't persist, but it's more complex contractually.
[05:12] Sana: For HIPAA equivalency — do you sign a BAA? Even though we're financial, some of our products trigger healthcare-adjacent requirements.
[05:20] Maya: Redwood can sign BAA for Private and Dedicated deployments; hosted requires legal review but we have customers with BAAs on hosted with scoping limitations. We'll include precedent redlines in the packet.
[05:31] Marcus: Good. Another question on incident response: in a breach scenario, what level of access do Redwood engineers have and can that be audited?
[05:41] Liam: Access is MFA + bastion with session recording. For Dedicated we provide just-in-time access with approval flows and you can require joint sessions. Session logs can be sent to your SIEM. For Private the access model is entirely under your control.

[06:20] Olga: Performance question — our target is roughly 4,000 requests per second during peak daytime. Latency SLO is 150 ms p95 for short prompts. What do you recommend?
[06:35] Liam: For that throughput we typically recommend Dedicated with autoscaling GPU pools, or Private if you need complete isolation. A40 or A100 class machines with continuous batching and prefix cache usually hit 100-200ms p95; H100 reduces latency but increases cost. We'll run an actual cost/latency estimate for your workload.
[06:58] Maya: We'll include cost modeling in the follow-up.

[08:05] Marcus: About model artifacts — do you allow bringing-your-own-model (BYOM) and does that change residency?
[08:14] Liam: BYOM is supported on Dedicated and Private. For hosted, we host vetted models; BYOM can be allowed under Private. Importantly, model weights can be stored in your region and access controlled with your KMS.
[08:28] Sana: Regarding logs that include partial account numbers — banking policy says we must mask PANs and store masked versions only. How do you handle redaction?
[08:36] Liam: We recommend client-side redaction or tokenization before sending. Alternatively, Redwood can run an inline redaction transform but that requires config and has implications for latency and auditability. We'll include recommended approaches in the packet.

[10:00] Olga: Any constraints on retention of KV cache? We sometimes need ephemeral caches for re-ranking and those may contain tokens.
[10:10] Liam: Cache TTL can be set to zero to avoid persistence; in Dedicated we can configure the cache to reside only in memory and evict aggressively. Private gives you full control.

[12:20] Marcus: A practical thing — our procurement requires vendor assurances for data residency plus proof of controls. Do you have attestation docs?
[12:30] Maya: Yes — we'll include SOC2 Type II report, HIPAA mapping, penetration test summaries, and our EU data flow diagrams. For Dedicated customers we can include change controls and maintenance windows.
[12:45] Sana: Can you include a sample redaction policy for prompt-level PII and a sample retention policy for logs?
[12:52] Maya: Absolutely, we'll attach redaction templates.

[14:05] Olga: On the networking side, for Private PoC we need an IP allowlist and an expectation of port ranges for the runtime. Also, what about egress? We need to prove there is no unexpected egress to third party endpoints.
[14:16] Liam: For Private, all egress is under your network. For Dedicated, we can provide a whitelist of egress endpoints and an exported egress report. Ports are standard HTTP/GRPC ranges; we'll send a network connectivity checklist.

[16:00] (brief cross talk — soft audio; two people speaking)
[16:18] Marcus: How do you handle legal holds — if we have to preserve logs for litigation, can we lock an immutable archive?
[16:26] Liam: Yes, you can ship logs to your immutable archive (WORM-enabled bucket) and we can stop automatic deletion. For hosted we can integrate with your long-term archive but it takes additional legal steps.

[18:00] Olga: Are there any hidden items that usually pop up during enterprise onboarding?
[18:10] Maya: A few: breakout items are encryption in transit endpoints for telemetry, RBAC mapping to your SSO groups, and neighborhood tenancy (we'll clarify exact tenancy model). Also operational runbooks for data exfil scenarios.
[18:28] Sana: On RBAC, we need to ensure separation of duties — no single Redwood engineer can escalate and change production policies without two approvals. Is that doable?
[18:36] Liam: Yes, Just-in-time with approval flows and audit trails can be configured. We'll document process and examples.

[20:00] Olga: For demo/PoC scope — we'd like Redwood to provision a test endpoint in eu-west, run 500 RPS for 2 hours using a redacted sample corpus, and verify logs ship to our SIEM. Is that feasible?
[20:15] Liam: Feasible — we suggest Dedicated for accurate cost and environment parity; Private if you need control over network. We'll scope the PoC with a short statement of work.

[22:45] Maya: Quick recap and next steps — we'll send the compliance packet, network checklist, and a proposed PoC SOW. Liam will handle the cost/latency estimate. You will send traffic patterns, logging destinations, and compliance control list.
[23:05] Marcus: One more — can you provide a contact for legal to talk about BAA and DPAs?
[23:12] Maya: I'll include our legal contact and precedent redlines in the packet.

[23:40] (conversation shifts to small details and scheduling)
[24:00] Olga: Okay thanks everyone, we'll aim to get those artifacts over by next Tuesday.
[24:06] Maya: Thanks, appreciate it.

(Recording stops after follow-up scheduling and short clarifications; rest of the meeting was administrative.)
